{"id": "68:17/q09", "question": "Who were the garden owners by people, religion or kinship?", "turns_on": "Conflicting reports identify nationality, religion and historical period differently.", "positions": [{"id": "68:17/q09/p1", "position": "Heirs of a righteous father, commonly described as sons or brothers.", "reasons": "Muqātil calls their forebears righteous Muslims after Jesus; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls the heirs brothers. Some accounts name three sons, while Ibn ʿAbbās in Ṭabāṭabāʾī names five; these number reports are set out separately below."}, {"id": "68:17/q09/p2", "position": "Abyssinians or Ethiopians.", "reasons": "ʿIkrima and Ibn ʿAbbās relate a charitable father whose sons called him foolish and vowed to stop feeding the poor; al-Māwardī separately reports this identification."}, {"id": "68:17/q09/p3", "position": "People of the Book, without a fixed Jewish or Christian identification.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the father was righteous and believing, without specifying Jewish or Christian; Ibn ʿAbbās is cited by al-Ṭabarī, al-Naḥḥās and al-Durr."}, {"id": "68:17/q09/p4", "position": "Israelites, including an elder who gave away his annual surplus.", "reasons": "Qatāda's account gives the elder and sons; al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī report the identification as an alternative."}, {"id": "68:17/q09/p5", "position": "A Muslim man or family of Thaqīf in Yemen.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī attributes Thaqīf to the exegetes; al-Rāzī reports a Muslim Thaqīf owner near Ṣanʿāʾ."}, {"id": "68:17/q09/p6", "position": "A Jewish owner.", "reasons": "Some exegetes cited by Ibn ʿĀshūr reason from Jewish settlement in Yemen in or after Bilqīs's era and Torah tithes on fruit."}, {"id": "68:17/q09/p7", "position": "Unbelievers.", "reasons": "Al-Nasafī reports this from al-Ḥasan, while saying the majority held otherwise."}, {"id": "68:17/q09/p8", "position": "People living shortly after Jesus was raised.", "reasons": "Some exegetes date them before Christianity spread in Yemen; Ibn ʿĀshūr reports the proposed chronology near the Abyssinian conquest and Year of the Elephant."}]}
{"id": "68:17/q10", "question": "How many heirs were there?", "turns_on": "Different numerical reports.", "positions": [{"id": "68:17/q10/p1", "position": "Three brothers or sons.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawī and Bursawī give three heirs; ʿIkrima's report via Ibn ʿĀshūr calls them three wealthy sons."}, {"id": "68:17/q10/p2", "position": "Five sons, four supporting the plan and a moderate brother objecting.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī relays Ibn ʿAbbās's account of the unusually abundant harvest and the dissenting fifth brother."}]}
{"id": "68:17/q11", "question": "What had the father given to the poor?", "turns_on": "Accounts differ over surplus, gleanings and an owed share, which may coexist.", "positions": [{"id": "68:17/q11/p1", "position": "He kept his family's annual food and gave the surplus to the poor.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj also records this alongside gleanings; Qatāda describes the old man's sons objecting during his lifetime. Ibn Kathīr says the eventual loss covered crop, profit and charity."}, {"id": "68:17/q11/p2", "position": "He let the poor collect gleanings, missed fruit, fallen dates, grapes and what harvesting tools or wind left.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Farrāʾ, al-Baghawī, al-Bayḍāwī and others specify what pickers, sickles or wind missed. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says one account had the father bring the poor along at harvest; al-Wāḥidī says he announced it to them."}, {"id": "68:17/q11/p3", "position": "He paid God's due or gave a prescribed share to its rightful recipients.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās describes the poor's obligatory due; al-Qurṭubī says the Yemenite father paid God's due; Ibn ʿAbbās's report in Ṭabāṭabāʾī says each rightful person received a share."}]}
{"id": "68:17/q12", "question": "Why did the heirs plan to exclude the poor?", "turns_on": "Different reports emphasize household need or rejection of the father's charitable practice.", "positions": [{"id": "68:17/q12/p1", "position": "They feared their many dependents would be left short by continued giving.", "reasons": "Muqātil says they thought food plentiful yet had many dependents; al-Farrāʾ says wealth had shrunk. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says they judged his generosity mistaken."}]}

{"id": "68:17/q14", "question": "What did the oath resolve to do?", "turns_on": "Whether the oath is read only as intended harvest or also as an ominous literal cutting of the garden.", "positions": [{"id": "68:17/q14/p1", "position": "Harvest all the fruit secretly before the poor arrived, leaving them no share.", "reasons": "Muqātil says they would avoid announcing harvest as their father did; al-Ṭabarī, al-Baghawī and others describe dawn gathering. {"id": "68:17/q15", "question": "How is layasrimannahā related to the oath?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "68:17/q15/p1", "position": "It is the oath's response in reported third person; direct quotation would be first-person plural.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn supplies hypothetical lanasrimannahā; al-Ālūsī says the wording reports rather than quotes; Abū Ḥayyān calls it the oath response."}]}
{"id": "68:17/q16", "question": "What does ṣarm or layasrimannahā mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the word is explained by its ordinary harvest sense or its force of complete severance.", "positions": [{"id": "68:17/q16/p1", "position": "Cutting or harvesting fruit, especially date clusters, or gathering the crop.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī cites Imruʾ al-Qays using ṣaram for severing a relationship; Jishumī adds ṣarām and jadhādh for harvest and ṣarm for separation between companions. Al-Naḥḥās distinguishes jadhādh and says the verb means cut and gather; al-Wāḥidī and al-Qurṭubī explain aṣrama as palms ready for cutting. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ notes later figurative extension."}, {"id": "68:17/q16/p2", "position": "An emphatic complete severing of the garden that excludes the poor.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī hears finality in the expression; Elmalılı notes that their literal oath named cutting the garden itself."}]}
{"id": "68:17/q17", "question": "When was the harvest planned, and how does muṣbiḥīn work?", "turns_on": "Whether 'entering morning' emphasizes dawn itself or the dark period immediately before it.", "positions": [{"id": "68:17/q17/p1", "position": "At the beginning of morning or dawn, before the poor learned of it.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās and al-Samīn call muṣbiḥīn circumstantial; al-Samīn links it to the verb's subject and compares 37:137 and a proverb about a journeyer arrived by morning. Ibn ʿAṭiyya simply glosses entering morning. Al-Dāmghānī specifies dawn after the night has passed and relates the morning language to 68:20 and 18:42. Ibn al-Jawzī gives the basic sense of aṣbaḥa as reaching morning, while also recording its separate sense of kindling a lamp."}, {"id": "68:17/q17/p2", "position": "In late-night or predawn darkness while keeping the action secret.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī calls the dimness sadfa; al-Farrāʾ says late-night darkness; al-Zamakhsharī and al-Qurṭubī also put it before dawn."}]}
{"id": "68:17/q18", "question": "What did they fail to except from their plan?", "turns_on": "Whether the omitted exception concerns God's will in the oath or the poor's share of the harvest.", "positions": [{"id": "68:17/q18/p1", "position": "They did not say 'if God wills' when vowing about the future.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī explains that the conditional expression functions as an exception because their meanings coincide; al-Rāzī calls this the majority view and connects it to overconfidence. Jishumī says one cannot be sure a future statement will occur. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ rejects this as the verse's apparent gloss."}, {"id": "68:17/q18/p2", "position": "They intended to make no exception for the poor and leave none of the crop.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī reports this alternative; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ prefers the apparent story of taking everything at dawn over the divine-will formula."}]}

{"id": "68:17/q20", "question": "What happened to the orchard after the oath?", "turns_on": "Reports differ on the garden's physical fate and the origin of Ṭāʾif's name.", "positions": [{"id": "68:17/q20/p1", "position": "It burned or was blighted overnight and appeared black, ruined or reduced to ashes.", "reasons": "Muqātil says it perished; al-Māwardī gives ashes; al-Baghawī says the heirs found it black; al-Nasafī calls it a blight. Al-Zamakhsharī reports ṭayf beside ṭāʾif for the calamity and refers to 18:42; he lists ṣarīm as cut, blackened, dry, empty or sandy. The owners initially thought they had lost their way, then admitted deprivation through their wrongdoing."}, {"id": "68:17/q20/p2", "position": "Gabriel swept the garden around the Kaaba and set it at what became Ṭāʾif.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī reports this as an explanation for the town's name and fertility."}, {"id": "68:17/q20/p3", "position": "Ṭāʾif's name came instead from a man of Ṣadaf who built a wall around the town.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī transmits al-Bakrī's competing etymology."}]}
{"id": "68:17/q21", "question": "How do later phrases in the story describe the owners' conduct and response?", "turns_on": "Different later expressions locate the action, the warning, the confession and the hoped-for restoration.", "positions": [{"id": "68:17/q21/p1", "position": "Their secret departure aimed to deny the poor but left them deprived themselves.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī explains ḥard through withholding good, withholding milk, determination or speed; he cites a line of poetry and swift birds called ḥarād. Some proposed the plan, others accepted, opposed or silently approved; hence mutual blame."}, {"id": "68:17/q21/p5", "position": "Their words express hope for God's pardon and a replacement garden.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī notes readings of yubdilanā with and without doubling and glosses desire toward the Lord as hope for His good and pardon."}]}
{"id": "68:17/q22", "question": "What became of the owners afterward?", "turns_on": "Reports state different degrees of restoration or leave the final outcome unanswered.", "positions": [{"id": "68:17/q22/p1", "position": "They repented and were given a better garden.", "reasons": "Mujāhid reports this; al-Qushayrī says another account has God replace the garden, followed by a renewed secret harvest plan."}, {"id": "68:17/q22/p2", "position": "They became sincere and received al-Ḥayawān, with grape clusters requiring a donkey to carry.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī transmits this from Ibn Masʿūd."}, {"id": "68:17/q22/p3", "position": "Their ultimate destination is left unsettled.", "reasons": "When asked whether they were of Paradise or Hell, Qatāda said the question burdened him."}]}
{"id": "68:17/q23", "question": "How does this parable connect to its sūra and nearby verses?", "turns_on": "The sources relate the parable to nearby deniers, shared responsibility and ultimate punishment.", "positions": [{"id": "68:17/q23/p1", "position": "It continues the warning against proud, wealthy deniers while consoling the Prophet and urging patience.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr links the new parable to wealth and children in 68:14; Elmalılı links the oath to the earlier frequent swearer. {"id": "68:17/q24", "question": "When were the garden verses revealed?", "turns_on": "Whether verses 17–33 share the sūra's early Meccan setting and how that bears on Badr.", "positions": [{"id": "68:17/q24/p1", "position": "The sūra is early Meccan, but the garden passage may have been revealed separately in Medina.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī finds the sūra's overall Meccan setting clear but judges a Medinan origin for the seventeen garden verses plausible. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ excepts 17–33 and 48–50 from the early Meccan sūra and notes the traditional placement after al-ʿAlaq (96:1), despite ordering disputes. {"id": "68:17/q25", "question": "How does the preceding threat of a mark relate to the parable's warning?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "68:17/q25/p1", "position": "A report sees the mark on the nose as humiliation on Judgment Day for one who showed arrogance.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr reports this reading and mentions 3:106; the report belongs to the preceding threat, which the orchard warning follows."}]}

{"id": "68:17/q27", "question": "How do composition and story selection give this garden account instructive force?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "68:17/q27/p1", "position": "Qur'anic stories select useful material and place it in a fitting context to teach, admonish, and provide proof.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says stories serve higher purposes than amusement, select material for lessons and communal benefit, and gain force as proof and explanation in their sūra contexts; knowledge of earlier peoples also challenged People of the Book. He also distinguishes the plural qiṣaṣ, with kasra, from qaṣaṣ, with fatḥa, a verbal noun used for the narrated object."}]}

For the interpretation about their share, he says attachment to the harvesting oath is possible."}, {"id": "68:18/q01/p4", "position": "In the reading about the poor's share, it can attach to the time set for harvesting.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī gives this as an alternative attachment to the harvesting oath."}]}
{"id": "68:18/q02", "question": "What exception did the owners fail to make?", "turns_on": "Whether istithnāʾ qualifies the vow by God's will, excludes the poor's share, means reversal of resolve, or names a tasbīḥ formula; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ and Islahi contest the verbal-qualification reading on the story and the construction.", "positions": [{"id": "68:18/q02/p1", "position": "They did not qualify their oath or plan by God's will, such as saying 'if God wills.'", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Ṭabarī, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, al-Qurṭubī, and others give the formula in shāʾ Allāh. Mujāhid, reported by Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān, says they resolved as if they controlled the outcome; Abū Ḥayyān says al-Zamakhsharī follows him. Al-Rāzī and Kur'an Yolu call this the majority view, while Islahi reports the exegetes as unanimous but rejects it. Al-Biqāʿī includes any other phrase returning the matter to God's will. Elmalılı includes conditions such as reaching morning safely or suffering no accident, which their confidence overlooked. Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Ālūsī compare the sons with their father, who had set aside a share. Al-Ālūsī says the syntax apparently links this sense to their swearing."}, {"id": "68:18/q02/p4", "position": "Their omitted expression of exception was 'Glory be to God, our Lord,' or 'Glory be to God.'", "reasons": "Abū Ṣāliḥ, reported by al-Māwardī and al-Qurṭubī, gives subḥāna rabbinā; al-Durr reports his shorter wording subḥān Allāh. The reports vary in the formula's wording."}]}
{"id": "68:18/q03", "question": "Why can invoking God's will be called an exception?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "68:18/q03/p1", "position": "The qualification turns back or limits an absolute statement: a condition on God's will has the practical force of an exception.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī derives the forms from th-n-y, restraining or turning back, since the exception returns an oath to God's will; al-Rāzī and the Imam as reported by al-Ālūsī similarly say it suspends the oath's certainty or effect. Al-Jishumī distinguishes excluding a member of a general class from lifting a statement's ruling through God's will, including God's preventing or enabling the act. Al-Rāghib, quoted by Bursawī with 6:145, defines exception as removing part of a general statement or its ruling. Al-Bayḍāwī says the condition and exception are equivalent formulations of not harvesting until God wills; al-Nasafī, al-Zamakhsharī as reported by Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn, and al-Ālūsī likewise say the formally conditional in shāʾ Allāh functions as an exception. Al-Biqāʿī says it removes some of an oath's absolute force."}]}
{"id": "68:18/q04", "question": "Why does the clause use the present tense?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "68:18/q04/p1", "position": "It makes their failure vivid and signals that it was an error.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī contrasts the present form with the past tense expected in the narrative."}]}
{"id": "68:18/q05", "question": "What did the owners plan, and what led them to it?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "68:18/q05/p1", "position": "After inheriting a charitable father's garden, the sons planned a dawn or secret harvest that would keep the poor from receiving fruit.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ says their dependents had grown and wealth had shrunk, so they chose late-night darkness. ʿIkrima in al-Ṭabarī says their father fed the poor and the sons called him foolish; Qatāda says they opposed his charity. Al-Thaʿlabī explains their oath to cut the crop at dawn before the poor knew. Abū Ḥayyān reports that the father paid God's due; another account has him leave poor neighbors dates and grapes missed by harvesters, while the sons pleaded dependents. He explains their oath as secret early harvesting, whose response predicts cutting the crop. Ibn Kathīr says they wanted no poor person or petitioner to know and receive charity. Ibn ʿAbbās, reported by al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī, says the harvest was unusually abundant; five sons planned to withhold the Muslims' poor share, four agreed, and the moderate brother objected. {"id": "68:18/q08", "question": "What fault does this verse expose?", "turns_on": "The notes emphasize distinct, compatible grounds of blame: presuming control, planning to deprive the poor, and the culpability of evil intent.", "positions": [{"id": "68:18/q08/p1", "position": "They confidently treated the outcome as under their own control, without acknowledging God's will.", "reasons": "Mujāhid, reported by Ibn ʿAṭiyya, says they resolved as if they controlled the outcome. {"id": "68:19/q01", "question": "What does طاف عليها convey?", "turns_on": "The first explanation emphasizes the verb's circling image; Ibn ʿĀshūr additionally draws a sense of domination or descent from its preposition.", "positions": [{"id": "68:19/q01/p1", "position": "The visitation passed around and encompassed the entire orchard.", "reasons": "Al-Rāghib (via Bursawī) derives ṭawf from circling something, originally to guard it, and extends it to a night visitor, jinn, image, or servant. Ibn ʿĀshūr takes the literal circling as an image of calamity affecting every part of the garden, comparing 7:201; al-Ālūsī and Elmalılı likewise say it encircled the orchard. Al-Kalbī (via al-Wāḥidī) explicitly makes عليها refer to the orchard. Ibn al-Jawzī explains tawāf as movement around something that covers all its sides, and says Arabic can call a jinn that visits and circles people a ṭāʾif."}, {"id": "68:19/q01/p2", "position": "With على, the verb depicts the calamity as descending upon or taking control of the orchard.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr attributes this shade to the preposition على; al-Ālūsī also glosses the action as the affliction descending. {"id": "68:19/q02", "question": "What was the طائف that visited the garden?", "turns_on": "Reports identify the unnamed visitor by different agents or kinds of disaster, including competing origins for the fire; Ibn ʿĀshūr says the verse leaves its kind unspecified, and al-Ālūsī rejects the relocation account.", "positions": [{"id": "68:19/q02/p1", "position": "A divine calamity, punishment, scourge, or destructive visitation.", "reasons": "Muqātil, Qatāda as reported by al-Māwardī and al-Ālūsī, and many commentators identify a punishment or calamity; al-Samīn says ṭāʾif usually signals harm. Al-Qushayrī says it came from heaven and burned the fruits. Ibn ʿAṭiyya allows fire or another destructive agent; Ibn ʿĀshūr says its precise kind is deliberately unnamed, while 68:20 shows its ruinous effect. Al-Biqāʿī calls the act slight for God despite its devastating effect."}, {"id": "68:19/q02/p2", "position": "A command, decree, or event from God.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās calls it God's act or command in al-Ṭabarī, al-Māwardī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Qurṭubī, and al-Durr; Abū Ẓabyān transmits the wording 'a command from God's command.' Al-Zajjāj says the fire burned it all; al-Naḥḥās specifies its crops. Al-Kalbī via al-Wāḥidī says fire was sent from heaven; Ibn ʿAbbās via al-Wāḥidī says it surrounded and burned it. Al-Wāḥidī explicitly prefers Ibn ʿAbbās's account as the core explanation. Ibn ʿĀshūr also reports a fiery blast. Ibn al-Jawzī reports some exegetes' description of a scorching fire that swept over the garden."}, {"id": "68:19/q02/p4", "position": "A fiery column or tongue emerged from the garden's own valley and destroyed it.", "reasons": "Ibn Jurayj is reported with a neck or column of fire from the garden valley by al-Māwardī and with a tongue of fire from that valley by al-Ālūsī. {"id": "68:19/q03", "question": "Must a طائف come at night?", "turns_on": "Whether 7:201 and explicit daytime Arab usage defeat al-Farrāʾ's proposed nighttime restriction.", "positions": [{"id": "68:19/q03/p1", "position": "Yes: in ordinary usage a طائف is a nighttime visitor or event.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ gives the restriction and cites Abū al-Jarrāḥ's poem, 'I visited it by day, not at night,' as an explicitly exceptional expression; he says Arabs can use daytime visitation idiomatically for an impossible or unexpected event. {"id": "68:19/q04", "question": "How is طائف alternatively read?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "68:19/q04/p1", "position": "Al-Nakhaʿī reads طيف in place of طائف.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn, and al-Ālūsī transmit the reading; al-Samīn refers back to discussion of the two descriptions at 7:201."}]}

{"id": "68:19/q12", "question": "What lesson does the garden's loss teach?", "turns_on": "The sources draw consequences for provision, giving to the poor, and the Prophet's opponents from the same loss.", "positions": [{"id": "68:19/q12/p1", "position": "Sin can deprive people of provision already prepared for them.", "reasons": "Ibn Masʿūd transmits a Prophetic warning applying loss of provision to the owners' crop. {"id": "68:19/q13", "question": "What senses does al-Damghānī list for ṭayyib?", "turns_on": "This note concerns a separate lexical entry, not a word in 68:19.", "positions": [{"id": "68:19/q13/p1", "position": "The entry announces eight senses and lists lawful things, manna and quails, good food, clothing, sex, meats and fats, hoofed animals, slaughter, good provision, and good speech.", "reasons": "Al-Damghānī gives this list in his ṭayyib entry."}]}

{"id": "68:20/q02", "question": "What does كالصريم liken the ruined garden to?", "turns_on": "Which attested sense or referent of ṣarīm supplies the simile: darkness, a cut or barren state, dawn/day, ashes, sand, the named place, or the unusual gold gloss; the notes also differ over whether the trees themselves or only their fruit were removed.", "positions": [{"id": "68:20/q02/p1", "position": "A black, dark night: the burned garden was blackened.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba, al-Farrāʾ, al-Zajjāj and others tie the color to burning.
